title: Ravana and the brother who warned him
hookLine: Ravana lets one desire swallow everything, and sends away the brother who warned him.
carry: dharma, artha, kama: let none swallow the rest
tomorrow: one duty for everyone, or a different one for each?
last: WHAT PLEASES HIS PEOPLE IS GOOD.

lines: A BROTHER SAYS: GIVE HER BACK.
HE IS SENT AWAY. LANKA FALLS.
cards: Ravana has everything a king could want: golden Lanka, armies, wealth, pleasure. Then he carries off Sita, another man's wife, and Rama's army gathers across the sea.

In Ravana's court, his younger brother Vibhishana stands up and says what no one else will: give Sita back, and Lanka survives. Ravana calls him a traitor to his face. Vibhishana leaves and crosses over to Rama.
In the end the war takes Ravana's sons, his brothers, his city and his life. The Arthashastra itself names Ravana among the kings ruined because they couldn't master themselves.

teach.h: DHARMA, ARTHA, KAMA: THE THREE AIMS.
teach.b: Hindu teaching names three aims for a life in the world: dharma, doing right; artha, a living and the means to live; and kama, joy and love.
Together they're the trivarga, and with moksha, release, they make the four purusharthas, the aims of a human life. The Arthashastra's chapter on the sage-king, the rajarshi, says how they fit.
He isn't asked to give up joy.

teach.h: ENJOY, BUT NOT AGAINST THE OTHERS.
teach.b: He should enjoy life, as long as it doesn't go against dharma or artha.

teach.h: ONE PUSHED TOO FAR HARMS ALL THREE.
teach.b: Or he gives all three their due together, because they're bound to one another. Push any one too far, the text warns, and you harm it, and the other two with it.
That's Ravana in one line: one desire, and the pride that wouldn't give it up, pushed past dharma, cost him his wealth, his family and every joy he had.

teach.h: ARTHA CHIEF; TEACHERS STOP THE KING.
teach.b: Then Kautilya adds that artha alone is chief, because dharma and kama depend on it. One fair reading: chief means the floor the others stand on, not the only aim.
And the chapter doesn't trust even a sage-king to keep the balance alone. His teachers and ministers, it says, should stop him when he goes wrong. Ravana had that brother, and sent him away.

how: Hindu teachers speak of dharma, artha and kama as aims of a householder's life, often with moksha beside them. Ravana's fall in the Ramayana is told as the classic warning of one aim swallowing the rest.

o: an old ruling book's start: three aims balanced, artha their floor
an old ruling book's start: wealth is the only aim worth having
an old ruling book's start: a king must give up every pleasure

p: the brother who said: give Sita back
harms itself and the other two
dharma and kama depend on it
stop the king when he errs

s: the Arthashastra's ideal king gives up all pleasure
he enjoys life, as long as it doesn't go against dharma or artha; he shouldn't live without happiness.
it calls artha chief because the other aims depend on it
chief as the floor, not as the only aim: a kingdom must eat to live rightly or happily.
Ravana thanked Vibhishana for warning him and changed course
he called his brother a traitor; Vibhishana went over to Rama, and Lanka fell.

games.q: a friend's dad is opening a second restaurant. he works every night, misses his kid's games and his mother's puja, and says 'it's all for the family.' by the sage-king chapter, what's going wrong?
o: nothing. artha is chief, so work comes first, always.
one aim is swallowing the other two. artha is the floor, not the whole house.
he should close the restaurant. wealth itself is the problem.
games.why: Kautilya calls artha chief because dharma and kama depend on it, and warns that one aim pushed too far harms all three.

practice: Bring to mind the one person most likely to tell you, kindly, that you're wrong: a parent, a teacher, an old friend.

In many Hindu homes, elders and teachers are greeted with folded hands and a bow; in your mind, greet this person that way. Breathe slowly with their face in mind. If you pray, ask to hear them when it matters.
If you don't, just thank them silently, one breath at a time.

wordCard.voice: The Arthashastra's opening: the sage-king who keeps dharma, artha and kama in balance, and lets his teachers stop him.

orig.note: Sanskrit rajarshi, a royal sage: raja, king, joined with rishi, sage.

carryVoice: For the road: dharma, artha, kama, let none swallow the rest. Ravana let one swallow all three. Day fifteen ninety-one.

sources.ref: Arthashastra 1.7 (the rajarshi; enjoying desires without violating dharma and artha; the three aims interdependent; Kautilya: artha is chief; teachers and ministers to restrain the king)
Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Vibhishana urges Ravana to return Sita, is rebuked as a traitor, and goes over to Rama)
Arthashastra 1.6 (kings ruined by lack of self-mastery; Ravana named among them)
